---
order: 7
unit: guide
title: Open and close
summary: "An overview at the start tells the reader where a whole text is going, and a conclusion at the end tells them where it went. They are the topic sentences of the whole text. A good overview even sets the order of the paragraphs that follow."
language: maths
node: [AC9E7LA04 n2]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The overview names the net and the garden, the body paragraphs take them in that order, and the conclusion echoes both without adding anything new." }
hook: "A friend gives you directions: turn left, go past three houses, turn right. Would it help if they first said 'It's the blue house at the end of the next street'?"
---
A topic sentence tells the reader what a **paragraph** is about. A whole text has the same thing on a bigger scale:

- An **overview** (or introduction) at the start says what the text is about and where it is going.
- **Body paragraphs** each take one part, in order.
- A **conclusion** at the end pulls it together, so the reader knows where they have been.

## Predict: which helps more?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to how much an overview helps before seeing one makes its job concrete."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A report starts straight in with 'A female lays one to three eggs in a burrow.' Another starts with 'This report looks at three surprises about the platypus.' Which gets the reader ready faster?"
  options: ["The one that says what the report will look at", "The one that starts with a fact", "Both are the same", "Neither: the title does that job"]
  actual: "The one with the overview. The fact on its own leaves the reader asking whose eggs, and why we are talking about them. The overview says what is coming, so every fact has a place to go."
```

## Try: label the parts

```step
stage: run
insight: "Labelling each paragraph's job (overview, body, conclusion) shows that each block guides the reader in a different way."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 470 }
hint: ["Click a paragraph, then choose its job.", "The overview names what the report will cover. The conclusion pulls the three surprises together."]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "Which paragraph names the three surprises before any of them is explained?", options: ["The first", "The second", "The last"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The second explains one surprise: the eggs.", "The last pulls the surprises together after they have been explained."], explain: "The first paragraph is the overview: it names the three surprises the report will cover." }
check: { type: board, text: "Label each paragraph as the overview, a body paragraph or the conclusion.", when: "n_right = 5 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "The first paragraph names the three surprises. The middle three take one surprise each, and the last pulls them together without adding anything new." }
```

Were you right about the overview? It named the three surprises before the body paragraphs explained them.

## Worked example: what each part does

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Modelling how to check an overview against the body paragraphs and the conclusion gives a method for the whole text. Nib's slip is a conclusion that adds a new point."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What does an overview do for the reader?"
      options: ["Says what the text is about and what it will cover, often in order", "Gives the most interesting fact first", "Repeats the title", "Says what the reader should think at the end"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A good fact can hook a reader, but the overview's job is to show the way.", "It goes further than the title: it names the parts.", "That is closer to a conclusion's job, in a persuasive text."]
      explain: "The overview is a map: what the text is about and the parts it will cover."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is the plan for Nib's report, one paragraph per line. Click the paragraph that does the wrong job for its place."
      answer: 5
      fault: logic
      misconception: new-idea-in-conclusion
      explain: "Line 5: the conclusion brings in a new fact (wombats have cube-shaped droppings) that no paragraph covered. A conclusion pulls together what the text has already said. A new fact belongs in a body paragraph."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why might a conclusion repeat some words from the overview?"
      options: ["So the reader sees the text has come back to where it started", "Because the writer ran out of ideas", "To make the text longer", "Conclusions should never repeat the overview"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It's a deliberate move, not a lack of ideas.", "Length isn't the reason.", "A conclusion that echoes the overview ties the text together. It shouldn't copy it word for word."]
      explain: "Echoing the overview tells the reader the journey is complete: this is the point the text set out to make."
```

### Checking a whole text

```worked
\text{Read the overview} :: What is the text about? What parts does it promise to cover, and in what order?
\text{Match the body} :: Does each body paragraph take one of those parts, in that order?
\text{Read the conclusion} :: Does it pull the parts together, with nothing new?
\text{Fix what's missing} :: Add a missing overview, reorder the body, or move a new fact out of the conclusion.
```

Now: what does an overview do for the reader?

## Vary: put it in order

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Reordering a shuffled text by following the overview's own order shows that the overview sets the order of the body."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 470 }
hint: ["Click a paragraph, then use Move up and Move down.", "The overview names the surprises in an order: eggs, electricity, venom. The body paragraphs should follow it."]
check: { type: board, text: "Put the paragraphs back in order: overview, the three body paragraphs in the order the overview names them, then the conclusion.", when: "in_order = 1", explain: "The overview promised eggs, then electricity, then venom. When the body follows that order, the reader always knows which part they are in." }
```

## Practise: a persuasive text

```step
stage: practise
insight: "A persuasive text uses the same parts with a different flavour: the overview states a position, and the conclusion asks the reader to act."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 450 }
hint: ["First label each paragraph, then put them in order.", "The overview gives the reasons in an order: healthy food, then learning. The conclusion asks for something."]
check: { type: board, text: "Label each paragraph, then put them in order.", when: "n_right = 4 and in_order = 1", explain: "The overview states the position and two reasons, the body paragraphs take them in the same order, and the conclusion asks the principal to act." }
```

## Make: open and close it yourself

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing the overview and conclusion for body paragraphs that already exist makes students do the guiding work themselves."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#make", height: 470 }
hint: ["Click the empty first paragraph and type an overview: what the text is about and the two parts it covers, in order.", "Click the empty last paragraph and write a conclusion that pulls both parts together, with nothing new. Then label all four."]
check: { type: board, text: "Write an overview and a conclusion for the two body paragraphs, then label all four parts.", when: "n_empty = 0 and n_right = 4", explain: "Your overview tells the reader what is coming and your conclusion tells them where they have been. Read just your two paragraphs: do they make sense together?" }
```

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Checking a longer piece of class writing for an overview that matches its body is the transfer step."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In a longer piece of my own writing, I checked that the introduction says what the text will cover, the body paragraphs follow that order, and the conclusion adds nothing new. I fixed one thing that didn't match." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that an overview (introduction) tells the reader where a
  whole text is going, body paragraphs each take one part in that order, and a
  conclusion pulls it together with nothing new. They label paragraphs by their
  job, reorder a shuffled text by following its overview, and write an overview
  and a conclusion for given body paragraphs.
time: 45
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 10 min · Vary 6 min · Practise 8
  min · Make and own writing 13 min
goals:
  - I can say what an overview and a conclusion do for a reader.
  - I can check that the body paragraphs follow the overview's order.
  - I can write an overview and a conclusion that guide a reader through my text.
struggle: "Students often write a conclusion as a last new fact, or an overview
  that just repeats the title. Point them to the job: map at the start, pull
  together at the end."
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: click each paragraph and choose its job.


  The one idea: the overview and conclusion are the topic sentences of the whole
  text. This is AC9E7LA04 node 2 (structural cohesion devices), which depends on
  node 1 (topic sentences), the previous lesson.


  The platypus facts are checked against general reference sources (egg-laying,
  electroreception, the male's venomous spur). The persuasive text and Nib's
  wombat report are written for the lesson.
running:
  - "Predict: ask what a reader does with a fact when they don't know what the
    text is about."
  - "Try: ask which words in the overview tell you the conclusion is coming back
    to it."
  - "Worked example: Nib's cube-shaped droppings are a great fact in the wrong
    place. Where should it go?"
  - "Vary: the overview sets the body's order. Ask students to point to the
    words that decide it."
  - "Make: read only the overview and conclusion aloud. Do they make sense as a
    pair?"
stuck:
  - see: A student's overview repeats the title.
    ask: What parts will your text cover? Can you name them in order?
    fix: "Add the parts: 'This text explains what a rip is and what to do if one
      catches you.'"
  - see: A student's conclusion adds a new fact.
    ask: Did any body paragraph say that?
    fix: Move the new fact into a body paragraph, or leave it out.
  - see: A student can't decide the body order in Vary.
    ask: What order does the overview name things in?
    fix: Follow the overview's order.
stretch: Write a different overview for the platypus report that names the
  surprises in a different order. Then reorder the body to match.
support: "A card: Overview = map. Body = one part each, in the map's order.
  Conclusion = pull it together, nothing new."
leads: >
  Next in Holding writing together: what goes inside a strong paragraph (claim,
  evidence and explanation).


  Every subject's extended writing (science reports, history explanations) uses
  this structure. Reuse the Make step's frame in other classes.
exit:
  q: A conclusion says 'Sharks have been around for 400 million years.' No
    paragraph mentioned this. What is wrong?
  a: It adds a new fact. A conclusion pulls together what the text already said;
    the new fact belongs in a body paragraph.
explain: >
  An **overview** at the start says what the text is about and what it will
  cover, often in order.


  Each **body paragraph** takes one part, in the order the overview gave.


  A **conclusion** pulls it all together, often echoing the overview, and adds
  **nothing new**.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Do short texts need an overview and a conclusion?
    prompts:
      - Would a three-sentence email need one?
      - How long does a text have to be before a reader gets lost without one?
    notes: Short texts often use one sentence for each (the topic sentence and a
      closing line). Longer texts need whole paragraphs. The job is the same.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Directions without the destination
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Read out step-by-step directions to a place in the school without saying
        where it is. Then say the destination first and read them again.
      notes: Knowing the destination makes each step easier to follow. That is what an
        overview does.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Overview and conclusion only
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Students read only their overview and conclusion aloud. The class says
        whether they sound like a matching pair.
      notes: A good pair echoes the same words or ideas without copying.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: What's its job?
      type: question
      q: "'In this report, I will explain how volcanoes form and why they erupt.'
        Which part of a text is this?"
      options:
        - Overview
        - Body paragraph
        - Conclusion
        - Title
      answer: 0
      explain: It says what the report will cover and in what order, which is an
        overview's job.
```

# Texts for "Open and close" (cohesion board, parts mode, one block per paragraph).
# The s lines are in the right order with their roles; start: sets a shuffled order.

# region: run
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
s overview: The platypus is one of the most unusual animals in the world. This report looks at three of its surprises: it lays eggs, it finds food with electricity, and the males are venomous.
s body: Unlike almost every other mammal, the platypus lays eggs. A female lays one to three eggs in a burrow and keeps them warm by curling around them.
s body: A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nose closed. Its bill can sense the tiny electric signals made by the muscles of shrimps and worms.
s body: Male platypuses have a sharp spur on each back leg. The spur can deliver venom that is very painful to people, though it has not killed anyone.
s conclusion: Eggs, electric senses and venom make the platypus a puzzle that scientists are still studying. Next time you see one in a creek, you will know just how unusual it is.
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
label: off
tools: order
s overview: The platypus is one of the most unusual animals in the world. This report looks at three of its surprises: it lays eggs, it finds food with electricity, and the males are venomous.
s body: Unlike almost every other mammal, the platypus lays eggs. A female lays one to three eggs in a burrow and keeps them warm by curling around them.
s body: A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nose closed. Its bill can sense the tiny electric signals made by the muscles of shrimps and worms.
s body: Male platypuses have a sharp spur on each back leg. The spur can deliver venom that is very painful to people, though it has not killed anyone.
s conclusion: Eggs, electric senses and venom make the platypus a puzzle that scientists are still studying. Next time you see one in a creek, you will know just how unusual it is.
start: 4,2,5,1,3
# endregion

# region: practise
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
tools: order
s overview: Our school should start a vegetable garden. A garden would give students healthy food and a new way to learn.
s body: First, a garden means fresh, healthy food. The canteen could use our tomatoes, beans and herbs, and students would be more likely to eat food they grew themselves.
s body: A garden is also a place to learn. Science classes could study soil and plant growth, and maths classes could measure beds and record harvests.
s conclusion: Healthy food and real learning are two strong reasons to dig in. We ask the principal to give us one corner of the oval to start our garden next term.
start: 3,1,4,2
# endregion

# region: make
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
tools: text
s overview:
s body: Many Australian beaches have a rip current: a strong channel of water flowing away from the shore. Rips can look calm, with fewer waves breaking, which is why swimmers walk into them.
s body: If you are caught in a rip, don't swim against it. Float, raise an arm to signal for help, or swim parallel to the beach until you are out of the current.
s conclusion:
# endregion

# region: make-solution
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
s overview: Rip currents are one of the biggest dangers at Australian beaches. This text explains what a rip is and what to do if one catches you.
s body: Many Australian beaches have a rip current.
s body: If you are caught in a rip, don't swim against it.
s conclusion: Knowing what a rip looks like, and how to float or swim out of one, could save your life.
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
answer: on
s overview: Our new playground has two big changes: a climbing net and a quiet garden.
s body: The climbing net stretches between two poles and holds twenty students at once.
s body: The quiet garden has benches and shade for anyone who wants a calm lunch.
s conclusion: With the net for busy days and the garden for quiet ones, the playground now suits everyone.
# endregion

# The plan for Nib's report on wombats, one paragraph per line. Students click the paragraph doing the wrong job.

# region: nib
Overview: Wombats are strong diggers with a clever way to protect themselves. This report covers their burrows and their tough back end.
Body: Wombats dig burrows up to 30 metres long, with tunnels and rooms.
Body: A wombat's rump is tough, so it can block its burrow with its back end.
Body: When a predator chases it, the wombat dives into its burrow and plugs the entrance.
Conclusion: Wombats also have cube-shaped droppings, which is very strange.
# endregion
